description: Every time we make a hard thing disappear, we take away the chance for our kid to learn something I think is really important: hard doesn't mean I can't do it. This week's episode of the Good Inside podcast is all about raising a confident kid, and I think you're going to love it. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: I saw this video and wanted to jump in, because I think so many paren...
description: I saw this video and wanted to jump in, because I think so many parents are feeling this right now. The problem with gentle parenting isn't really the word gentle at all. It's that it usually skips this part entirely: boundaries. Gentle parenting was never supposed to mean no boundaries. Caring about your kid's feelings and stepping in to stop them can happen at the same time, and usually both need to happen. But womewhere along the way, a lot of us learned that validating our kid’s feelings and holding a boundary were opposites. When your kid is out of control, the most loving thing you can do is be the adult who takes over. It won't look gentle from the outside, and that's okay. Video credit: @oliviaeherman

title: Am I preparing the road for my kid, or am I preparing my kid for the ...
description: Am I preparing the road for my kid, or am I preparing my kid for the road? It's a question I don't think we ask enough. So often, in the name of love, we smooth things out for our kids. We step in before they hit a wall. We create an exit ramp the second something gets hard. It feels protective in the moment, but it can quietly send a message we don't intend: that hard things are dangerous, and that someone else needs to handle them for you. This week's episode of the Good Inside podcast is part of our partnership with @carters on The Childhood Confidence Project, giving parents real, practical ways to build confidence that isn't dependent on winning, being liked, or things going right. Real confidence isn't built by removing every challenge. It's built by kids getting the chance to sit with something hard and realize they can handle it, with us right there for support, not rescue. Listen to the full episode wherever you get your podcasts. #Carters_Partner #ad

title: My thoughts on gentle parenting on @callherdaddy. The problem with ge...
description: My thoughts on gentle parenting on @callherdaddy. The problem with gentle parenting isn't really the word gentle at all. It's that it usually skips this part entirely: boundaries. Somewhere along the way, a lot of us learned that validating our kid’s feelings and holding a boundary were opposites. That if we cared about how they felt, we had to bend. And if we held the line, we had to ignore how they felt. They’re not opposites. They’re two separate jobs, and you’re allowed to do both at the same time.

title: Your teen walks in the door after school, and before their shoes are ...
description: Your teen walks in the door after school, and before their shoes are even off they're checking Instagram or Snapchat. Part of you might be thinking, you were just with these people all day, what could you possibly have missed? I've caught myself having thoughts like that too. But for our kids, there isn't really a moment when the day with their friends ends. It keeps going, in their pocket, into their room, sometimes late into the night, and that's not something they did wrong, it's just the world they're growing up in. So it might help to think less about the phone itself and more about where there's still room in their day to be off it. A car ride with no screens, yours included. A walk to pick something up. Making dinner next to each other. You probably won't see anything change right away, and you might just get a shrug or a one word answer. That's okay. You're not looking for a big conversation, you're just making sure there are a few minutes here and there where no one else's opinion is coming in first, including yours. I go into this on my new episode of Teens & Screens, my series for parents trying to figure out tech with their kids. You can watch the full episode on YouTube now.

title: When your kid tells you something hurt, or scared them, or wasn't fai...
description: When your kid tells you something hurt, or scared them, or wasn't fair, it's so tempting to jump straight to "you're fine" or "it's not a big deal." We say it because we want them to feel better. But "I believe you" can do so much more. You don't have to agree with every detail or fix anything, you're just letting them know their experience is real, and over time that's how they learn to trust it themselves. This was such a great conversation with Kate Bowler. The full episode of the Good Inside podcast is out now, you can listen or watch at the link in my bio.

title: If you can't tell how you're feeling until you've checked how your ki...
description: If you can't tell how you're feeling until you've checked how your kids are feeling, you're not alone, and it comes from such a loving place. So many of us are giving our kids the kind of attention we wish we'd gotten growing up. But your kid's hard moment doesn't have to set your mood for the whole day. You're allowed to be okay while they're upset, and that's part of what helps them get through it. The full episode of the Good Inside podcast with Kate Bowler is out now. Link in bio. I think you'll really like this one.

title: At the end of a hard day, it's so easy to replay the meltdown or the ...
description: At the end of a hard day, it's so easy to replay the meltdown or the fight at dinner and decide the whole day was a failure. I catch myself doing this too. Tonight, before you go to sleep, try thinking of one moment, even a tiny one, when your kid laughed or leaned into you or just seemed okay. You don't have to pretend the hard parts didn't happen. You're just letting the good part count too. My full conversation with Kate Bowler on the Good Inside podcast is out now. Link in bio.

title: I have big news I've been excited to tell you about... I partnered wi...
description: I have big news I've been excited to tell you about... I partnered with @carters to make the confidence program totally FREE. Confidence is one of my favorite topics to talk about. Why? Because I think we've got it backwards. We're often taught that confidence is about feeling good about yourself. Being the best at things. It's not. I know that's a bold statement, but I think it's an important one. True confidence has less to do with feeling good and a lot more to do with self-trust. Knowing what you feel, believing it's real, and feeling okay being you while it's happening. That self-trust is strongest when kids are little, and it starts to dim as they get older. As a fixture in childhood for 161 years, Carter’s knows that firsthand - that’s why they’re teaming up with us for The Childhood Confidence Project to give you practical ways to help kids hold onto it. My confidence program is the first piece: short videos, the exact scripts of what to say to your kids, plus a LIVE workshop with me on October 14th where I'll take your questions about confidence. And it's all free thanks to Carter’s. I can't think of a more important time to build our kids' confidence than right now. Head to the link in my bio to learn more. #Carters_Partner #AD

title: So many of us treat happiness, for our kids and for ourselves, like s...
description: So many of us treat happiness, for our kids and for ourselves, like something we can earn if we just get enough things right. This conversation with Kate Bowler really made me rethink that. If happiness depends on a lot of things lining up at once, then some days they just won't, and that doesn't mean you did something wrong. It might just mean the small good things deserve more of our attention than we give them. The full episode of the Good Inside podcast is out now. Link in bio.

title: Some mornings, certain situations require M&Ms just to get out the do...
description: Some mornings, certain situations require M&Ms just to get out the door... there I said it. 😅 Thank you @callherdaddy for the fun conversation. You can listen to our full episode at the link in my bio

title: There's a moment in my conversation with Chris Voss, the former FBI h...
description: There's a moment in my conversation with Chris Voss, the former FBI hostage negotiator (@thefbinegotiator), that I keep coming back to. He talked about what to do when your kid screams "I hate you," and it's not to defend yourself, it's to get curious. "You hate me?" Not because the words don't sting, but because that curiosity is what keeps him from spiraling into being offended, and if you're offended, you're no good to the person in front of you. Hear the rest of our conversation on the Good Inside podcast.

title: I have good news for you. Being a parent really comes down to just tw...
description: I have good news for you. Being a parent really comes down to just two jobs: setting a boundary, validating the feeling. That's it. Nobody tells you that setting a boundary isn't a one time event you get right and then move on from. It's the same blocks, the same five year old, the same moment, probably tomorrow, and the day after that, and you doing the same two jobs all over again. I used to take that repetition personally, like if my kid needed the boundary again, I must have done something wrong the first time. Now I think about it differently. The repetition is the work. That's what's actually building the skill, for both of us, one wash, one rinse, one repeat at a time. So if you're on day thirty of the same blocks fight, you're not behind. You're right on schedule. This is exactly why I built my boundaries program. It includes video lessons, scripts, and practical guides that walk you through both jobs so they actually start to stick, not just for one hard moment but for the next thirty. Enroll now and you'll also get access to my live workshop on September 23 at 11am ET, plus the replay so you can watch anytime. You can learn more at the link in my bio.

title: When we parent for the short-term, our goal is often to “fix” the sit...
description: When we parent for the short-term, our goal is often to “fix” the situation, avoid disappointment, or make our kids happy. While well-intentioned, this approach actually robs our kids of building the skills they need to manage the inevitable difficulties of life. Instead, let’s parent for the long-term. Are you with me? Let’s share this reframe far and wide. Good Inside is only a movement because *you* help move these ideas around the world. Thank you @callherdaddy for having me on. Listen to our full conversation wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Why don't you ever listen to me? Why won't you put your phone down? H...
description: Why don't you ever listen to me? Why won't you put your phone down? Half the time those aren't really questions, they already have a verdict attached. Chris Voss, the former FBI hostage negotiator I sat down with for this week's Good Inside podcast, explained why "why" backfires: we're all conditioned since we were toddlers to hear it as an accusation. True in hostage negotiations, true at your kitchen table. Hear the rest of our conversation with @thefbinegotiator on the Good Inside podcast.

title: "Empathy is not approval." That's the distinction Chris Voss, the for...
description: "Empathy is not approval." That's the distinction Chris Voss, the former FBI hostage negotiator (@thefbinegotiator), walked me through on this week's Good Inside podcast: you can be curious about why your kid did something and still disagree with it. "Before I disagree, let me see if I got this right." Hear the rest of our conversation on the Good Inside podcast.

title: Every day, as parents, you’re the pilot of your family’s plane. You m...
description: Every day, as parents, you’re the pilot of your family’s plane. You make decisions - about bedtime, screens, snacks, toys - that your child might protest. Your child’s protest doesn’t mean you’re doing something wrong. It means you’re doing something important. As much as they protest, your child doesn’t actually want to fly the plane. They want to know you’re in control, even when they’re shouting from the passenger seat. Deep down, we all feel safest when someone says: “I know you’re upset. And I’ve still got this.” That’s what sturdiness looks like and it’s what build trust in the long-run. Thank you @callherdaddy for having me on. You can listen to our full conversation wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Have you made a decision in your house today, and not checked whether...
description: Have you made a decision in your house today, and not checked whether your kid was okay with it first? Bedtime, screens, dessert, even dinner. Take a second and actually think about it. If you're struggling to come up with an example, you're not alone, and it's not because you're a pushover. It's because somewhere along the way, a lot of us started treating our kid's buy-in as the thing that makes a decision okay to make. Here's the part I think gets missed: kids don't actually want that much power. It's heavy. When we hand them a vote on things that are ours to decide, we're not making them feel respected, we're making them carry something they're not built to carry yet. This is exactly what my new program is built around: what a boundary actually is, how to set one without it turning into a negotiation, and why time outs and empty threats don't work long term. It comes with on-demand video lessons, scripts, and practical guides you can start using the same day. Enroll now and you'll also get access to my live workshop on September 23 at 11am ET, plus the replay so you can watch anytime. Learn more at the link in my bio.

title: On my @callherdaddy episode I talked about confidence and what actual...
description: On my @callherdaddy episode I talked about confidence and what actually builds it in kids... and I wanted to expand on one piece of that here, because I keep thinking about it, not just as a parent but as a woman. How many times in my own life did I feel like something was off, or too much, or not right for me, and then someone told me I was overreacting, and I believed them over myself. That voice doesn't go away when we grow up. It just gets quieter and harder to trust. "You're so dramatic." "You're fine." In the moment, it seems like a harmless comment. But comments like that teach kids that other people know their feelings better than they do. So when I catch myself saying "you're fine" or "you're so dramatic" to my own kid, I try to remember what's actually happening underneath. Underneath that moment, my kid is really asking one thing. Can I trust what I feel, or does someone else get to decide that for me. "You're fine" answers no. "Tell me more" answers yes. Where do you notice yourself doubting your own read on things, even now, as an adult? I'd love to hear in the comments.

title: Have you ever caught yourself on a video or a voice memo, heard yours...
description: Have you ever caught yourself on a video or a voice memo, heard yourself say "okaaaaaayyyyyyy?" right after telling your kid something was happening, and thought, wait, when did I start doing that? I had to have someone point mine out to me before I could hear it myself. Once you notice it, you start hearing it everywhere, in your own house, in other people's kitchens, on the sidelines of a soccer game. It's such a small habit, barely even a sound, and it undoes basically everything you just said. The good news is you don't have to catch every single one. You just have to catch the next one.

title: If you feel like you're negotiating every single decision in your hou...
description: If you feel like you're negotiating every single decision in your house lately, you are not alone. I used to think good parenting meant having an airtight explanation ready for every rule. What actually changed things in my house was something much simpler: fewer words, said with more certainty. There's nothing wrong with your kid for testing that. And there's nothing wrong with you if you're worn down enough to want to just give in. You just need a few sentences ready before you're standing in it, and that's exactly what I made this video for. Three sentences matter most: that the decision's already made, that your kid doesn't have to like it, and that you're allowed to stop talking about it for now. And if you want more support putting these into practice, the exact scripts and scenarios, not just the theory, my brand new boundaries program walks you through it. Enroll now and you'll also get into my live workshop with me on September 23, plus the replay. More info at the link in my bio.

title: Sibling fights are rarely about the thing they're fighting about. And...
description: Sibling fights are rarely about the thing they're fighting about. And sometimes the hardest thing for a kid is to talk about what's really going on with a sibling head-on, so we look for a side door instead. That’s why a show that features siblings, like @gabbysdollhouse, can be exactly that. Watch it together, then say something simple after, low stakes, no lesson attached: “Huh. Sometimes a little sister feels sooo good, and sometimes it can feel sooo hard.” You probably won't get a profound reply. You might get silence. You might get "can I have a snack?" That's okay, I promise it still landed. Because now your kid knows it's okay to feel mad at a sibling, and a feeling that's allowed to exist out loud is a lot less likely to come out sideways later, in a hit, a slammed door, an “I hate you.” Next time you put on a show, if it touches something real in your kid's life, let go of the guilt. You might be doing the most useful parenting of your whole day. #NetflixPartner

title: You've said "last warning" more times tonight than you can count, and...
description: You've said "last warning" more times tonight than you can count, and by the third one, you both know it doesn't mean anything. Here's what I've learned, as a psychologist and as a mom who's said "last warning" too: warnings ask your kid to change their behavior before anything actually happens. Boundaries don't ask anything of your kid at all. They're about what you're going to do. That shift changes everything. A boundary doesn't need your kid's cooperation to work, which means you can stop negotiating and start acting, and you can stay close to your kid while they're upset about it instead of managing their reaction. This is exactly what's inside my brand new boundaries program. It's full of scripts and strategies for the moments that repeat most: bedtime, screens, siblings, the pushback before anything's even happened. Enroll now and you'll also get into my live workshop on September 23 at 11am ET, plus the replay if you can't make it live. Link in bio to sign up. A warning that doesn't hold isn't just a rough night. It's proof to your kid that nothing you say is final.

title: I'm still thinking about this moment from my conversation with @misty...
description: I'm still thinking about this moment from my conversation with @mistyonpointe. She was told to paint her skin to match the rest of the corps, and she described feeling invisible and hyper-visible all at once. Both true, at the exact same time. On this week's episode of the Good Inside Podcast, Misty and I talk about this exact moment, the mentors who taught her to advocate for herself, and what confidence looks like once you stop having to prove it. Hear the rest of our conversation on the Good Inside podcast.

title: Prince, parenting, ballet and everything in between. My full conversa...
description: Prince, parenting, ballet and everything in between. My full conversation with @mistyonpointe is out now on the Good Inside podcast now.

title: Have you heard the term "decision fatigue"? Hear my full conversation...
description: Have you heard the term "decision fatigue"? Hear my full conversation with Lauren Smith Brody in the final episode of our 3-part series on the Rattled podcast with @caredotcom. Listen wherever you get your podcasts!

title: @mistyonpointe spent decades training her body to hit an exact positi...
description: @mistyonpointe spent decades training her body to hit an exact position, night after night, under bright lights, in front of judges who noticed everything. And what she said next is the part that stuck with me: becoming a mother made her realize all that discipline was never really about control. It was about building enough stability in her body and her training that she could handle whatever happened once she actually stepped on stage, because so much of it was never hers to control in the first place. I think about this so much as a parent. We build routines and structure not because we're trying to guarantee a certain outcome, but because that structure is what gives us the steadiness to handle the moment we didn't see coming. On this week's episode of the Good Inside Podcast, Misty and I talk about this exact tension, between having a plan and needing everything to go according to it, and what ballet taught her about being ready to improvise instead.

title: @itsmissjazzy if you're seeing this: you are such a light for these k...
description: @itsmissjazzy if you're seeing this: you are such a light for these kids. Starting kindergarten is hard for kids, and it might be even harder for the parents. The energy you bring into that classroom is exactly the kind that helps families feel okay letting go. Thank you for your joy. I also know that sometimes videos we see online can bring up a little bit of "why doesn't my house look like that" for a lot of us. And that's such a normal feeling. My days don't always have that built-in positivity either. But here's what I'm choosing instead: I'm not going to say I can't do that. I'm going to say, I can probably do a piece of that. Maybe I can't build a whole classroom, but I can handwrite a couple affirmations for my kid's wall. Maybe I can't do all of this, but I can make our morning schedule visual so I'm not expecting my kid to just remember what comes next. So Miss Jazzy, and every teacher like you: thank you for the love you pour into our kids. And thank you for the reinvigoration too, the reminder that I can't run my house exactly like this classroom, but I can take a few pieces of it.

title: I saw this video from @katstickler about quiet time after school, and...
description: I saw this video from @katstickler about quiet time after school, and I loved it so much. I'm sure a lot of you will relate too, that pull to jump in with a hundred questions the second your kid gets in the car. If you're wondering why "how was your day?" so often gets a "fine" it's because your kid hasn't switched from school mode to home mode yet. School mode is armor. All day, they're reading the room, managing their face, figuring out where they stand, that takes real effort we don't always credit them for. Home mode is where the armor comes off. And that switch doesn't flip the second they leave the building. It flips when their body decides it's safe enough to let go of the day. So next time you get a "fine," maybe just let it be fine for a minute. The rest tends to show up on its own. 💛

title: I've been sitting on this news for weeks and I can finally share it. ...
description: I've been sitting on this news for weeks and I can finally share it. 🎉 Good Inside and KidStrong are officially partnering, and this is unlike anything we've done before. For the first time, Good Inside isn't just showing up for parents, we're showing up for kids too. I'll be bringing the Good Inside method to all KidStrong locations, right there on the blue floor. Each KidStrong class combines brain, physical and character challenges, led by highly trained coaches who understand what kids are up against. It's not just about strong bodies. It's about kids who believe they can, which perfectly aligns with Good Inside's goal to help you raise capable, resilient kids. Here's why this really matters to me: your kid can hear "you can do hard things" from you at home. But when they hear that same message from their coach mid-challenge, something clicks. Same language, everywhere they turn. That's how resilience actually sticks, when the message at home and the message everywhere else, line up. To kick things off: for a limited time, KidStrong members get 3 months of Good Inside membership free. What you're doing at home and what they're doing on the blue floor, finally speaking the same language. Head to the link in my bio to book your trial today. Together, we're raising kids who are strong inside and out.

title: I saw a video this week with a comment underneath it that stopped me:...
description: I saw a video this week with a comment underneath it that stopped me: "Your trauma may not be your fault. Healing is your responsibility." And I couldn't stop thinking about how much this applies to parenting too. So many parents ask me some version of: can it just be my kid's fault? Can they just own it? And I get it, because if it's your kid's fault, you're off the hook. But fault was never a useful question to begin with. Here's the distinction I actually care about. It's not your fault your kid is struggling. It never was. But you're still the one with the power to shift the environment, to try something different, to lead your family somewhere new. That's not a punishment, it's actually a vote of confidence. I trust parents to do this work more than I trust a four-year-old or a fourteen-year-old to do it on their own, and that's not a knock on the kid, it's just true. Where does the fault versus responsibility distinction land for you? Tell me in the comments. Video credit: @whispersofwow

title: 5 of my hot takes as a clinical psychologist. ⬇️ Let me know which on...
description: 5 of my hot takes as a clinical psychologist. ⬇️ Let me know which ones you agree with. 1. Validating your kid’s feelings without holding a limit doesn’t build regulation. It builds a kid who falls apart the second the answer is no. 2. It’s ok to say no to your child. You don’t have to turn it into a “creative yes.” Kids are going to hear no in the real world. Let’s not have them hear that word for the first time at age 19. 3. No one ever says, “I’m so proud of my 25-year-old, she just does everything everyone asks of her, compliant and smiling all the time.” So let’s stop glorifying it in a 5-year-old. 4. Most of us think we’re setting a boundary when we're actually making a request. “Please stop jumping on the couch” is a request. Standing up and taking your kid off the couch is a boundary. Yes, your kid will be upset about it. That’s ok. 5. Entitlement is fear of frustration. It builds in a kid who gets an exit ramp every time something is hard: a call to change their class so they can be with their best friend, a screen at their sibling’s soccer game that they find “boring,” permission to quit the team because they’re no longer a starter. Tell me - What're your unpopular parenting opinions?

title: 📣 Keep your brilliant ideas to yourself! I know that sounds counterin...
description: 📣 Keep your brilliant ideas to yourself! I know that sounds counterintuitive but hear me out.... I think most of us grew up believing that being a good parent means having the answer ready. Your kid struggles, you swoop in, problem solved, everyone feels better for a second. Here's what took me a long time to see. Every time I do that, I'm not actually helping my kid, I'm just proving to them that the good ideas live in *me*, not in *them.* And they feel that, even if neither of us says it out loud. Self trust doesn't come from a childhood free of struggle. It comes from a kid sitting in the messy, uncertain middle of a hard problem and coming out the other side with something, anything, that was theirs. My job isn't to hand over the win. It's to be a steady presence while they find it themselves, even when every part of me wants to jump in. Where do you catch yourself stepping in too fast? Tell me in the comments.

title: Raise your hand if you had rules you swore you'd keep before you actu...
description: Raise your hand if you had rules you swore you'd keep before you actually had kids, and then didn't... 🙋‍♀️🙋‍♀️🙋‍♀️ This clip from @sooootruepod had me laughing and thinking about how many things I swore I'd do as a parent before I had kids. Tell me in the comments - What is something that you have done as a parent that you swore you'd never do? Remember, there's never any judgment here. Video credit: @sooootruepod

title: How do you emotionally prepare to leave your baby for the first time?...
description: How do you emotionally prepare to leave your baby for the first time? After having a baby, it's normal to feel anxious about this. You might wonder if what you're feeling is normal, if you're leaving too early, or how long is the "right" amount of time to be away. You want certainty that you're doing it right. Here's the truth: there's no single right answer. But there are strategies that can help you manage the anxiety that comes with this step. Listen to episode 2 of our new 3-part series on the Rattled podcast with Care.com, all about new parenthood and childcare. Available wherever you get your podcasts.

title: If back to school is stirring up big feelings, in your kid and in you...
description: If back to school is stirring up big feelings, in your kid and in you, you are not alone. New teacher. New routine. New everything. Of course this feels like a lot. And underneath all of it, your kid is looking right at you to figure out how worried, or anxious, or excited they should be. I used to think my job in these moments was having the right facts ready or the perfect explanation. What actually helped my own kids more was something simpler: staying calm near them and letting them borrow that calm for themselves. There's nothing wrong with your kid for needing that. And there's nothing wrong with you if you don't always feel calm enough to give it. You just need the right words for the right moment, and that's exactly what I made this video for. Three moments matter most this week: before you leave the house, at drop off, and at pickup. And if you want more advice from me on what to say beyond the first day of school including those inevitable rough mornings and the homework battles, my brand new Back-to-School program walks you through it. Register now and you'll also get into our live workshop with me on August 19, plus the replay. Link in bio.

title: Our kids go through difficult stages - yes, my kids too! When there’s...
description: Our kids go through difficult stages - yes, my kids too! When there’s hitting, kicking, biting - these are some of the most challenging moments we face. And yet often, we end up intervening in ways that - while 100% well-intentioned - can lead to more rather than fewer problem behaviors. I spent two hours in a Reddit thread called "Nothing Works," reading real questions from parents in the thick of it. So I recorded a full episode of the Good Inside podcast answering them, including exactly what to do when your kid won't stop hitting. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Hitting, biting, throwing - aggressive behavior is a signal, not a ba...
description: Hitting, biting, throwing - aggressive behavior is a signal, not a bad-kid problem, and here's what actually helps. I spent two hours in a Reddit thread literally called "Nothing Works" and recorded an episode answering real questions from that thread, including what to do when your kid won't stop hitting. You can check out the full episode of the Good Inside podcast wherever you get your podcasts.

title: “How do I know what the right childcare is for my baby?” Every parent...
description: “How do I know what the right childcare is for my baby?” Every parent asks some version of this. And underneath the question is something so tender: I love this baby more than anything, and I need to know I'm not getting this wrong. We want a guarantee. A green light. Some magic answer that will finally make us sure. Here's the real answer: there is no one perfectly right choice. There's no caregiver who will do it exactly the way you do it, and there's no decision that comes with a guarantee. There is just a thoughtful parent, making the best call they can with love and good information. I'm exploring this, and so much more, in Episode 1 of a new 3-part series on the Rattled podcast with Care.com on new parenthood and care. Listen wherever you get your podcasts. #CarePartner

title: "But mom, I'm the ONLY ONE" Pretty much every teenager has said this ...
description: "But mom, I'm the ONLY ONE" Pretty much every teenager has said this line or a variation at some point, but it means something you may not realize. It sounds like your teen is angry, but they actually might be scared. Here's a teen translation ⬇️ What they say: "I'm the ONLY ONE" What they mean: "I'm scared to be alone, I want to belong" Dr. Sheryl and I dive into this on the latest episode of our YouTube series, Teens & Screens. We'll give you scripts and real advice on how to handle these tough conversations with your teens. Watch the episode on Good Inside's YouTube channel.

title: Do you remember getting dressed for school as a kid? The uniform you ...
description: Do you remember getting dressed for school as a kid? The uniform you hated, the shoes that had to be tied "just right," the fights over a jacket you swore you didn't need? Turns out our kids are having the exact same battles with us now. Good news: these moments are predictable, which means they're fixable, with the right tools. That's why I built my Back-to-School Program. It's full of scripts, tools, and strategies, like the "outfit station," for the moments that actually get hard: mornings, drop off, school refusal, homework battles, the whole transition. And if you enroll now, you also get into my live workshop on August 19 (plus the replay, so you're covered either way). A hard start to the school year isn't just a hard day. It's a tax on the whole house that builds for weeks. Link in bio to get started.

title: Attempting to potty train this summer? Potty training is one of the f...
description: Attempting to potty train this summer? Potty training is one of the first times kids learn whether they are in charge of their own bodies. So the words we use during the process matter. I teamed up with Pampers and their Peppa Pig Easy Ups to show you a few easy ways you can build your kid’s confidence throughout the learning process. For example, instead of saying, “You’re amazing! YAY!” try: “You did it.” Why is this swap so important? When your reaction is more level, your kid learns to feel motivated from the inside rather than depending on your praise. You can also add in a familiar face, like Peppa Pig to make the process more playful and friendly. When kids feel playful and safe, it’s their best chance to learn. P.S. Go to the link in my bio for my free Potty Guide in Good Inside - it has all the things you need to feel confident about potty training! #PampersPartner

title: I thought we could all use a laugh this weekend. 😅 Your turn… what’s ...
description: I thought we could all use a laugh this weekend. 😅 Your turn… what’s the sickest burn your kid has said to you lately? I'll go first. Thanks for the honesty @sterlingkbrown @kellyclarksonshow

title: Morning breakfast battles are rarely about the food. They're about co...
description: Morning breakfast battles are rarely about the food. They're about control. Your kid wakes up and the whole day has already been decided for them: what they're wearing, when they're leaving, what's happening at school. Breakfast is one of the only moments where they get a say. So give them the say, just inside a container that works for you. And this can be fun, like the morning menu I use with my kids. Give them three options, written down the night before. It's enough agency to feel like a decision, not enough chaos to blow up your morning. Back-to-school season is here and I think this can help make all our mornings a little smoother. This type of strategy is exactly what's inside my brand new Good Inside Back-to-School program. I made it to help you feel more supported through the moments that make or break the start of the year: drop off, meltdowns, homework battles, routines. The program also comes with a live workshop on August 19 at 12PM ET. If you can't make it live, you can still get the recording. Link in my bio to sign up.

title: Anxiety gets such a bad reputation, but it's actually trying to help ...
description: Anxiety gets such a bad reputation, but it's actually trying to help you. It increases your alertness because your body thinks something in your environment needs extra attention, and when you have a new baby, that's often true. The nuance is this: waking up wondering if you fed your baby recently makes sense. Waking up to a ten alarm fire every single time, even for things that aren't actually threats, is something else. That's the difference I get into on this week's Good Inside podcast with Dr. Chris Choukalas. Watch it wherever you get your podcasts.

title: You'd never call a parent selfish for not playing peekaboo while fend...
description: You'd never call a parent selfish for not playing peekaboo while fending off a bear. But that's exactly what Dr. Chris Choukalas was going through after his daughters were born, his nervous system stuck in protector mode, with no bandwidth left for bonding. On the surface, this is a story about one dad. But the more we understand what's actually going on underneath behavior, our own or someone we love, the more that behavior starts to make sense, and the more we can actually do something about it. Listen to the full conversation on the Good Inside Podcast.

title: Parents, does this sound familiar? Turns out that's not annoying, it'...
description: Parents, does this sound familiar? Turns out that's not annoying, it's actually good news. Kids love correcting us because it's one of the only times they get to feel like the expert instead of us. And you can use it: give your kid a slightly wrong version of their day, and watch them can't help but correct you with the real details. 😂 Try it one day this week and let me know how it goes. Video via @libby.ronon @libby.Tobin

title: Boundaries are not what we tell kids not to do; boundaries are what w...
description: Boundaries are not what we tell kids not to do; boundaries are what we tell kids we will do. This is such an important distinction to provide the framework for you to effectively set and hold boundaries with your kids.   When you set boundaries, you're saying: *I'm the adult. I'm in charge. I can handle this. You're safe.* That's what creates psychological safety.   The hardest part of all this? Your kid probably won't thank you. They won't say, "Wow, I'm so glad you held that boundary and let me have my feelings." They'll probably be upset for a while. They might say you're mean. They might say you don't care.   But what they're actually learning - what their nervous system is taking in - is: *My parent loves me. My parent can handle me. My parent won't let me fall apart. I'm safe.*

title: Parents of toddlers often ask me: "This situation keeps happening, an...
description: Parents of toddlers often ask me: "This situation keeps happening, and by the time it does, I'm at a five-alarm fire. What do I do then?"   My answer is usually the same: there's very little we can learn about ourselves or change when we're already at an emotional 10.   Whether you're parenting a toddler or leading a team at work, it helps to understand your road to reactivity. When we can identify those moments ahead of time, we can prepare differently. We can build in support. We can respond with intention instead of reacting from overwhelm.   Emotional regulation isn't about staying calm in every difficult moment. It's about understanding what leads you there in the first place.   What helps you stay grounded when work gets stressful? I'd love to hear in the comments.   Loved my conversation at LinkedIn with Jessi Hempel. You can watch the full conversation on my LinkedIn.

title: If you’re thinking about potty training - or as I call it, potty *lea...
description: If you’re thinking about potty training - or as I call it, potty *learning*, I want you to remember: PP! Patient and Playful. As the parent, you get to set the tone, and when you bring that patient and playful energy to the process, your kid knows that they’re in a safe place to learn.   But PP also stands for my old friend, Peppa Pig. When kids see their favorite characters in the process or on their Pampers Easy Ups, it can make the whole process feel a little less intimidating.   Remember: There will be accidents, but perfect isn’t the goal. Perfect isn’t even a thing. This is a chance for your kid to build independence and own the process.   P.S. Head to the link in my bio for my free Potty Guide in Good Inside - it’s everything you need to feel confident going into the process! #PampersPartner

title: Your child throws cards everywhere when they lose a board game… Storm...
description: Your child throws cards everywhere when they lose a board game… Storms off of the soccer field when the other team wins… or won’t participate if they aren’t guaranteed a win..   In these moments, something unmanageable is happening in their body; for many kids, losing brings up feelings of not-good-enough-ness, and the big reaction on the surface is a response to these painful feelings, not to the loss itself.   So it makes sense that being a "good loser" isn't something they can just decide to do, it's something they need your help regulating through. That's where emotional vaccination comes in: infusing connection into these moments before they even happen. Try it before your next Pictionary game night, and let me know how it goes in the comments.   This video is part of an ongoing partnership with Netflix.

title: Hot take: boundaries aren't about controlling your kid.   In a family...
description: Hot take: boundaries aren't about controlling your kid.   In a family system, I think about roles, or even "jobs," like this: parents establish safety through boundaries, validation, and empathy. Children explore and learn, through expressing their emotions and wants.   Boundaries aren't a one-time thing you introduce when the stakes get high, they're a muscle you and your kid build together, starting small. If the first boundary you ever set is around phones and social media, your kid isn't just upset about the phone, they're upset because you've never said no before, and now you're doing it with the thing that feels like their whole world.   I talk more about boundaries and screen time in my new series I created on YouTube called Teens & Screens. You can check it out on the Good Inside YouTube channel.   If you're parenting a tween or teen, I hope you'll watch. And I hope you give me feedback, what felt helpful, what felt too-far-from-realistic-to-be-helpful, what do you want me to cover next.

title: Being a "good girl" teaches you to gaze out. You become an expert on ...
description: Being a "good girl" teaches you to gaze out. You become an expert on your environment, reading the room, tracking everyone else's needs, staying a step ahead of whatever might upset someone. And somewhere along the way, you often learn that your worth, your value, even your safety, is tied to meeting those needs.   Belle Burden knows this well, she was nicknamed "Belle the Good Burden" growing up. On this week's episode, we talk about what happens when the life you built around being "good" stops protecting you. I can't wait for you to hear our full conversation. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Belle Burden, author of Strangers, wrote publicly about the sudden un...
description: Belle Burden, author of Strangers, wrote publicly about the sudden unraveling of her long marriage during the early days of the pandemic. But what about what was going on for her as a mom, and for her kids, during that time?   Hear the full conversation on this week's episode of the Good Inside Podcast wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Belle Burden was "Belle the Good Burden" growing up. And I think we a...
description: Belle Burden was "Belle the Good Burden" growing up. And I think we all know what that means. Easy. Compliant. Follows the rules. Maybe even the "favorite child." A lot of us were that kid, too.   On this week's episode of the Good Inside Podcast, Belle and I spent a lot of time talking about the concept of being a "good girl" and how Belle is shedding that nickname once and for all. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Everyone tells you that having a baby is supposed to be the happiest ...
description: Everyone tells you that having a baby is supposed to be the happiest time of your life. And then your baby arrives... and instead of feeling nothing but joy, you feel overwhelmed and disoriented. And worst of all, not like yourself.   It's so easy to make that mean, "What's wrong with me?"   In my conversation with Dr. Sekhon on Rattled, she shared a phrase for this feeling that I haven't stopped thinking about: hormonal whiplash. Sometimes there's so much comfort in having language for an experience that can feel so confusing.   If this part of new parenthood feels familiar, I hope this conversation helps you feel a little less alone. Listen to the full episode wherever you get your podcasts.

title: It's chemistry, not character.   When you are having big emotions pos...
description: It's chemistry, not character.   When you are having big emotions postpartum, I want you to remember that those feelings are a chemical, hormonal response to the stress of being a new parent.   Dr. Sekhon breaks down the hormonal whiplash your body goes through on this week's episode of Rattled. Listen now wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Half of teenagers are on their phones between 12AM and 4AM. Read that...
description: Half of teenagers are on their phones between 12AM and 4AM. Read that again. So it's no wonder your teen seems emotionally dysregulated during the day, can't focus, or feels like a completely different kid than they used to be. I know how that lands. Some of you are thinking, "Is it too late for us?" I promise it's not too late. I sat down with my colleague, Good Inside teen expert Dr. Sheryl Ziegler to talk through exactly this topic in our brand new series we're bringing to YouTube. We go over what's actually happening during those hours, and what you can do about it. I can't wait for you to watch.

title: I am SO excited to finally share this with you. I'm teaming up with G...
description: I am SO excited to finally share this with you. I'm teaming up with Good Inside teen expert Dr. Sheryl Ziegler to make something we both wish existed years ago: Teens and Screens. A new series on YouTube where we go deep on what's actually going on for teenagers and technology - not to scare you, but so you can understand your kid and know what to actually do. If you have a teenager, you already know: telling them to get off their phone doesn't work. It usually just ends in a fight, a slammed door and more disconnection. Here's what I've learned: the phone isn't the whole problem. It's what's happening to your teen's brain, sleep, and nervous system because of the phone that's actually driving so much of the behavior you're seeing at home. This isn't another "just set better boundaries!" video. It's the real information behind why those boundaries are so hard to set in the first place.

title: I recently shared a video about my "Side-Door Strategies" - and so ma...
description: I recently shared a video about my "Side-Door Strategies" - and so many of you asked for more. So here's a deeper explanation. If this resonates, feel free to share it or save it for later.   If this resonates, feel free to share it or save it for later.   Front-Door Strategies are direct, intentional, and straightforward. You walk right up to the problem and name it head-on. You might say: "I know you're upset that you didn't make the team" or "Hey, let's talk about what happened with your sister."   But for Deeply Feeling Kid front-door strategies often backfire. Why? Because there's a level of shame and fear that makes direct approaches feel too intense, too exposing. When you walk through that front door, your DFK slams it in your face: "Stop talking!" "Get away from me!" "Leave me alone!"   Side-Door Strategies are indirect, creative, and sneaky-in-the-best-way. Instead of walking straight at the problem, you meander around it. You might say: "You know, if *I* didn't make the team, I'd probably feel really upset" or you talk to your kid while driving in the car where eye contact isn't required, or you let them hide under a pillow while you share something vulnerable.   If this sounds like your child, if you’re looking for more support, I’ve got you covered with my Deeply Feeling Kids Program. Link in bio for more.

title: Reminder for new moms: YOU JUST GREW AN ENTIRE HUMAN BEING!   This we...
description: Reminder for new moms: YOU JUST GREW AN ENTIRE HUMAN BEING!   This week on Rattled, I sat down with Dr. Lucky Sekhon, a reproductive endocrinologist, to talk about the hormonal whiplash of pregnancy and postpartum.   Listen to the whole conversation wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Not taking accountability comes from shame. Keep watching for a quick...
description: Not taking accountability comes from shame. Keep watching for a quick script for how to handle these moments.   If this is striking a chord, I got you covered. I'm doing a live Deeply Feeling Kid workshop in Good Inside on July 22 at 2pm ET. In the workshop, I will address what's going on and what these kids need from us; I will share concrete approaches to build regulation + more peace in your home + self-care. Link in bio for all the details.

title: This happened to me last year and I remember the reaction was palpabl...
description: This happened to me last year and I remember the reaction was palpable. SO many of you said you had a child just like this. Here’s the thing. Some kids feel things deeper, more intensely, and for longer than other kids. These Deeply Feeling Kids are amazing kids. They are strong, they know how they feel, they aren’t swayed by people-pleasing tendencies. These kids are going to change the world. AND: these kids need a different parenting approach. We have to get close but not too close so we don’t activate their sense of threat, we have to see their goodness under their bad behaviors, and we must put up firm boundaries so they don’t feel they overpower us. I love these kids, I understand them, and I know exactly how to help. If you (like me!) have a DFK and haven't taken this workshop yet - now is the time. I'm hosting a live Deeply Feeling Kids Workshop on July 22. Link in bio to sign up.

title: Here’s the thing: some kids feel things deeper, more intensely, and f...
description: Here’s the thing: some kids feel things deeper, more intensely, and for longer than other kids. These Deeply Feeling Kids are amazing. They are strong, they know how they feel, and they aren’t swayed by people-pleasing tendencies. These kids are going to change the world.   AND - these kids need a different parenting approach. We have to get close, but not too close, so we don’t activate their sense of threat. We have to see their goodness underneath their difficult behaviors, and we must set firm boundaries so they don’t feel like they overpower us.   I love these kids, I understand them, and I know exactly how to help.   If you (like me!) have a DFK and aren't a member yet - your timing couldn't be more perfect. My next Deeply Feeling Kid Live Workshop is happening on July 22. I truly believe this might be the thing you’ve been looking for to turn things around in your home. Link in bio to learn more.

title: Many kids with ADHD are also Deeply Feeling Kids.   They’re easily ov...
description: Many kids with ADHD are also Deeply Feeling Kids.   They’re easily overwhelmed, shut down when upset, and often push away help when they need it most. Typical strategies can feel like “too much” - which is why things escalate instead of settle.   A lot of parents think, “This sounds like my kid… but they have ADHD - will this still help?” Here’s my answer: yes, and.   Yes, because these kids share many of the same core struggles and benefit from a different, “side door” approach. And, this doesn’t replace therapy, school supports, or medication. It works alongside them. There’s nothing wrong with your child. They just need a different approach. If you watched this video and thought, “Sounds like my kid…”, head to the link in my bio to learn more about our Deeply Feeling Kids (DFK) program to better understand and support your child.   I hope this feels helpful. I’m sharing it as support, not to replace medical or therapeutic advice. Good Inside does not diagnose or treat medical or developmental conditions. If you have concerns about your child, I always encourage you to connect with a qualified professional.

title: Most of us try to connect to our kid by “walking through the front do...
description: Most of us try to connect to our kid by “walking through the front door.”   That might sound like, “I get that you’re mad when your sister says you can’t play with her.” or “Hey, look at me…I’m not mad at you. I just want to help.”   These are all love phrases, and for many kids these phrases lead to connection. They’re essentially “Front-Door Strategies” because we approach our child directly, overtly name the feeling they’re experiencing, and clearly offer our support.   Well, our Deeply Feeling Kids need something else. Why? Because there’s a level of shame and fear that blocks their vulnerability and willingness to let you in. Our kids don’t want to be alone when they’re overwhelmed. They need our help. They just need it in a non-traditional way: they need Side-Door Strategies.   One way to do this is to shift the focus. Instead of suggesting how your DFK might feel: “Ugh, your sister said you can’t play with her? I get that you’re mad about that.” Name how someone or you might feel: “Ugh. If my sister told me that I couldn’t play with her, I feel like I’d be really mad. I’m not sure about you, just saying that’s how I’d feel.”   If you have a kid who reject the “typical” parenting strategies. They tend to push you away when they need you the most, or only get more upset you try to name their feelings. I have a feeling you too have a Deeply Feeling Kid.   If this sounds like your child, if you’re looking for more support, I’ve got you covered in my Deeply Feeling Kids 101 Program. Link in bio for more.

title: Hey parents, th enext time you feel like you did nothing today, remem...
description: Hey parents, th enext time you feel like you did nothing today, remember: you built a brain today. That's not nothing.   I sat down with Dr. Dana Suskind on the Good Inside podcast to explore how AI is reshaping childhood brain development and why human connection can’t be replaced by machines. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Kids don't just need connection, they need messy, friction-filled, hu...
description: Kids don't just need connection, they need messy, friction-filled, human connection to actually learn how to be human. An AI that's always there, always agrees, and always makes your kid feel like the center of the world teaches them one thing: that they're the only one who matters, and they never learn how to connect with anyone else. My conversation on this topic with Dr. Dana Suskind on the Good Inside Podcast is out now, listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: This is the reality of the world our kids are growing up in. And most...
description: This is the reality of the world our kids are growing up in. And most of us are asking questions like: is AI cheating? Should I limit screen time? How do I monitor what they're doing? Those aren't bad questions. But I don't think they're the right questions. And asking the wrong ones leads us down a road that feels reactive, overwhelming, and even kind of hopeless. There's a different way to think about this. One that actually leaves you feeling grounded in your values and confident in the kids you're raising.   This is such an important conversation, and I go deep with Dr. Dana Suskind on this week's episode of Good Inside. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Summer sounds amazing, right? No school, no structure, endless freedo...
description: Summer sounds amazing, right? No school, no structure, endless freedom. But for Deeply Feeling Kids, it's actually really hard. Your DFK thrives on predictability and routine. They know what to expect at school: the same teacher, the same classroom, the same schedule. Their nervous system can settle into that rhythm. Summer blows all of that up. No structure to lean on. All of that unpredictability is overwhelming for a kid whose nervous system is already absorbing everything around them.   One thing that helps: create micro-routines within the chaos. You don't need to schedule every minute of summer - that's not realistic and it's not the point. But you can build in small anchors of predictability. Maybe mornings always look the same: breakfast, get dressed, then you have freedom. Maybe there's always a quiet time after lunch. Maybe bedtime is non-negotiable. These small pockets of "I know what's coming next" help your DFK's nervous system settle enough to handle the unpredictability in between.   If this resonated, summertime is actually the perfect time to jump into my Deeply Feeling Kid Program. Link in bio for more.

title: Watching Wimbledon this week got me thinking about parenting Deeply F...
description: Watching Wimbledon this week got me thinking about parenting Deeply Feeling Kids. A great tennis player loses points all the time. They can even lose a set and still win the match. They're not playing for every single point, they're playing for the long game.   Parenting your DFK works the same way. Win the game, not the moment.   If this sounds like your kid, I've got you covered. My Deeply Feeling Kids Program includes a live workshop on July 22nd at 2pm where I'll break it all down. Learn more about the full program by going to the link in my bio.

title: Emmy Rossum said something on Call Her Daddy that I can't stop thinki...
description: Emmy Rossum said something on Call Her Daddy that I can't stop thinking about. She challenged the idea that moms can do it all and have it all - because when we actually pull it off, the thing we sacrifice is ourselves.   Here's what I'd add to this conversation. Being the mom who sometimes does a bit less isn't just okay for you. It's good for your kid. For a very specific long-term reason. So if you're seeing this and need permission to do a little less today, here it is. And if this resonates, send this to a mom who might need to hear it too.

title: If you're the one who hears the cry first, who's already up before yo...
description: If you're the one who hears the cry first, who's already up before your partner even stirs, you're not imagining it. If it's been a biological pregnancy, especially if you're breastfeeding, you have a head start bonding with your baby, and that can leave your partner feeling shut out, even useless. Here's the thing: dads often come into their own at a different stage, not the newborn haze, but later, when there's more to do together.   On this week's episode of Good Inside, I talked to neuroscientist Dr. Darby Saxbe about exactly this. Listen wherever you get your podcasts.

title: MGI = Most Generous Interpretation. If you’re like me, then when it c...
description: MGI = Most Generous Interpretation. If you’re like me, then when it comes to your kid’s or partner’s or colleague’s latest behavior, it’s always easier - and more natural! - to come up with an LGI (Least Generous Interpretation).   The power of MGI is that it forces us to see the good person under the bad behavior… and this never excuses the behavior, but rather sets the foundation for productive intervention and positive behavior change.   I get into this with neuroscientist Dr. Darby Saxbe on this week's episode of Good Inside, listen wherever you get your podcasts. I can't wait for you to hear this one.

title: There is NO such thing as a perfect parent. Share this reel with some...
description: There is NO such thing as a perfect parent. Share this reel with someone in your life, think we could all hear this important reminder a little more often.   Listen to my full conversation with Darby Saxbe on the Good Inside Podcast wherever you get your podcasts.

title: Is anyone else watching the World Cup and relating Erling Haaland to ...
description: Is anyone else watching the World Cup and relating Erling Haaland to parenting? Just me? 😂 He wanders around for a bit as if he's doing nothing, then out of nowhere, scores. Here's how relates to parenting. You're not trying to win every moment, you're trying to win the game. The next time your kid is melting down and you feel like you're doing 'nothing,' remember: that's not permissive, that's leadership. You're playing the long game, the one where they learn who you are and who they are, over months and years, not minutes.

title: Gloria Steinem invites you into her home to talk with a group of wome...
description: Gloria Steinem invites you into her home to talk with a group of women about one of the most pressing issues of your time.   I know. It sounds like the start of a riddle, or a once upon a time. But it happened. A few weeks ago.   The topic was raising kids in the age of AI. That sounds like some hyperintellectual problem, and you might be thinking, I'm just trying to survive tantrums and sibling arguments and sleep issues. But the dynamics underneath those everyday moments? They mirror everything we talked about. So the conversation wasn't up in the clouds at all. It was practical. Real. About the same things you're navigating at home every day.   And here's what stayed with me: in a moment when everyone's focused on what technology can do, we spent our time talking about values and relationships and the conditions we need to preserve to keep the human world feeling human.

title: This video from @mrsdsdiary made my week! Good Inside has been transl...
description: This video from @mrsdsdiary made my week! Good Inside has been translated into so many languages, shared between friends, passed from parent to parent - and that's not because of me. It's because of all of you.   If you're thinking of reading Good Inside, here's a helpful reminder: Think of this book as your handbook for parenting. Just like a reference guide, you flag up the chapters you need, as you need them. Then you can come back to new chapters as your child grows and develops. You won’t need every chapter at once, but you will need all of them at some point! I want to give you the tools that help you to embody your authority while fostering a parent-child connection - so you become the parent you want to be.   I hope it becomes a tool in your parenting tool belt that you refer to again and again. And if you've read it, what part resonated most for you? I'd love to know.
